title: The merkavah as craft observation
statement: The corpus reads Ezekiel 1 — the living creatures, the wheels within wheels, the crystalline expanse, the enthroned likeness — as a close eyewitness description of an Elohim craft and its party, the canon's own treatment naming it the most interesting craft description in the corpus of scripture; the mobile kavod ('glory') that departs and returns across Ezekiel 8-11 and 43 is read as a physical object rather than a metaphor, and the prophet's transports by the ruach ('the spirit lifted me up') as craft-borne conveyance — the single most operationally detailed theophany in the Hebrew Bible, read operationally.

includes: The craft reading of Ezekiel 1 as the canon states it, at the canon's own level of detail: observed hardware and personnel, a frightened precise observer, the scroll commission that follows

The mobile-kavod extension: the departures and returns of Ezekiel 8-11 and 43 read as one physical object's movements, which is what makes the book's structure an itinerary rather than a metaphor's development
The conveyance reading of the ruach transports

The reception registration: Ezekiel 1 as the seed-text of merkavah mysticism and the Hekhalot literature — registered as reception history, with the mystical tradition's own theology preserved to the tradition
excludes: Any engineering reconstruction of the craft; Blumrich's attempt is registered as an independent precedent of the reading, not adopted — the corpus endorses no schematic
The temple vision of Ezekiel 40-48 and its Embassy connection, which is woh-claim-0016's territory
The visionary-genre scholarship's own account displaced; the storm-theophany and Mesopotamian-iconography reading is carried against this record in full
Merkavah mysticism's theology, which is reception, not observation

source_references.locator: TBWTT-WOH 3:157-171, 'Les soucoupes volantes d'Ezechiel': the canon's verse-by-verse craft reading of Ezekiel 1-2, the service-craft gloss, the scroll commission
Ezekiel 1 (the inaugural vision); 3:12-15, 8:3, 11:1, 11:22-24, 43:1-5 (the transports and the kavod's movements)
Greenberg's philological commentary on Ezekiel 1 as the mainstream control: the vision within prophetic-theophany genre and its ancient Near Eastern iconographic vocabulary
Blumrich's independent craft-reading, registered as precedent and as cautionary case (the reconstruction required selective handling of the text)

alternatives.statement: Ezekiel 1 is prophetic theophany built from a known vocabulary — storm-cloud imagery, composite creatures, wheeled thrones of Mesopotamian iconography — fully explicable within its literary environment; the operational detail is the genre's grandeur, not a witness's precision.
The craft reading keeps the wheels and the platform but quietly drops the four faces, the eyes, and the likeness-of-a-man on the throne; it is literalism applied only where the text cooperates.

revision_triggers: Claim woh-claim-0016's handling of Ezekiel 40-48 changes in a way that reaches the kavod reading.
